analysis.one_liner: Reinstates the lapsed federal ban on large-capacity ammunition magazines and tightens it.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to a House Judiciary subcommittee in May 2007 and died there when the Congress ended, with one sponsor and one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The 1994 federal assault weapons ban, which outlawed ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds, expired in 2004. This bill would have brought that ban back into law and added new rules: it would make it a crime — punishable by up to 10 years in prison — to sell a semiautomatic assault weapon together with a large-capacity magazine, and it would require licensed gun dealers to certify to the Attorney General within 60 days whenever they sold a magazine made before the ban, so old stock couldn't be passed off as new. Retiring police officers could keep their service magazines. The bill was introduced in April 2007, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: The public broadly, if the ban's supporters are right that limiting large-capacity magazines reduces the number of casualties in mass shootings. Gun violence prevention groups supported this kind of measure, and law enforcement officers were given an explicit exemption to keep their service magazines after retirement.

how_it_helps.text: The bill reinstates the criminal provisions outlawing the possession or transfer of large-capacity ammunition feeding devices that were part of the 1994 assault weapons ban, which had been allowed to lapse [S2][S3].
It adds a new crime, punishable by up to 10 years in prison, for transferring a semiautomatic assault weapon together with a large-capacity magazine [S3].

It requires licensed manufacturers, importers, and dealers who sell pre-existing large-capacity magazines to certify to the Attorney General within 60 days that those devices were made before enactment, a paper trail designed to stop old stock from being sold as if it were newly legal [S2][S3].
It preserves an exception allowing a retiring law enforcement officer to keep a large-capacity magazine transferred to them upon leaving service [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Gun owners, who could no longer buy or transfer newly made large-capacity magazines; firearms manufacturers and dealers, who would lose a product line and take on a new certification requirement; and dealers who violate the certification rule could face up to five years in prison.

drawbacks.text: The bill criminalizes conduct that had been legal since the 1994 ban expired in 2004, and manufacturers and dealers would lose the ability to sell large-capacity magazines, facing fines and up to 5 years in prison for violating the certification requirement [S2][S3].

Millions of large-capacity magazines were already in private hands, so the bill could not remove those from circulation; a certification paper trail for old stock added compliance costs for dealers and created potential criminal exposure over paperwork [S3].

Critics of magazine bans argue their effect on overall gun crime is limited because most shootings involve few rounds, so the bill's benefits would be concentrated in rare mass-shooting scenarios — a point of genuine dispute among researchers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: gun owners and dealers lose access to a product, and the public gains a restriction aimed at reducing mass-shooting casualties. The bill was reasonably designed in one respect — it grandfathered existing magazines rather than confiscating them and exempted retiring police — but that same design choice means millions of large-capacity magazines would remain in circulation indefinitely, limiting how much the ban could accomplish. Whether the safety benefit justifies the burden on the firearms trade is the honest fight at the heart of it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn McCarthy of New York introduced the bill on April 16, 2007 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and on May 4, 2007, referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security [S5].
The bill had one cosponsor, a Democrat [S4].
No further action was ever recorded: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and dealers, who kept selling large-capacity magazines without restriction, and gun owners, who kept access to them. The public gained nothing, since no vote ever tested the idea.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearms makers, dealers, and gun owners

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded, so the partisan shape can only be inferred: the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were both Democrats, and the bill died quietly in a committee controlled by the Democratic majority.

industries.note: The bill would have outlawed making and selling large-capacity magazines to civilians, eliminating a product line. The industry's interest in keeping that market open runs against the bill's stated public-safety purpose.

Dealers would lose large-capacity magazine sales but keep a legal path to sell grandfathered devices, with a new requirement to certify pre-enactment manufacture to the Attorney General within 60 days of any transfer; failing that could mean fines and up to five years in prison [S2][S3].
